title: A new documentary series explores the history of US prisons
text:
A new documentary series explores the history of US prisons
Documentary director and filmmaker Lynn Novick’s 2019 directorial debut, “College Behind Bars,” examined the role of education in rehabilitating incarcerated individuals. That led her to want to understand the roots of the modern prison system. The result is “Crime and Punishment in America” (PBS, Nov. 16).
“I didn’t know the history at all, and I am glad I had the chance to learn it by making this film,” says Ms. Novick.
The Monitor spoke with the director over the phone. The interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
The Monitor interviewed filmmaker Lynn Novick about the making of “Crime and Punishment in America,” which was produced by Ken Burns.
Q: The way this documentary chronicles the history of crime and punishment in America is stunning. What kind of time and research went into organizing that history?
When I see a finished film, it’s hard to imagine what went into it. It’s kind of the tip of the iceberg, and everything that goes into it is underneath the surface. For every image you see [in the documentary], there are thousands of images that were considered, and that also goes for every piece of footage or every time someone [appeared] on camera. The research began with us going back to Colonial times, talking to historians about the state of justice in America as the country was becoming a nation, and then working our way through history up to today.
The way we approach [research] is that we keep a very open mind, and we don’t get too locked into the narrative until we’ve done the research. There’s a scene that begins our second episode, and it’s a story of a woman who was a photographer in California at the turn of the last century. She got a contract to photograph people who had been arrested in this town, and she took pictures of them, the way she took pictures of everybody else who came to the studio. So these are basically mug shots, but they don’t look like mug shots. I’m telling you all this, just to say that this is a good example of our research process.
We had sent an intern, Rosie Feerick, to a bookstore to look for books about crime and punishment, and she came back with this book called “Prisoners” by Arne Svenson. It was a collection of these images and the story of how they came to be taken and why they were preserved. It helped us raise a lot of profound questions. What if [people who committed crimes] were treated with a different approach? And what if the camera saw them differently? We might see them differently.
Q: This documentary features some prominent lawyers and activists such as Sherrilyn Ifill, Bryan Stevenson, and James Forman Jr. How important are their voices to a project like “Crime and Punishment”?
One of the central principles of the whole project was telling a story of institutions and systems that affect all of our lives and are very important in our society. We don’t tend to focus on it because a lot of what happens is far away from us and is inherently very impersonal. We wanted to always center the story on people and individuals whenever possible, and try to find individual stories that would help us gain some understanding of what these systems, institutions, and practices actually mean for people. With James Forman, Sherrilyn Ifill, and Bryan Stevenson, it was such an incredible privilege to sit down with those amazing humans and hear their perspectives. Then to drill down into the intimate personal stories and line them up was the challenge of the project.
Q: Beyond the data and narratives, there is care and concern for both the victims of violent crime and the overpoliced that shines through. Why was it important to take an empathetic approach?
I would hope that I am empathetic and compassionate to the people whose stories I tell in every film I’ve worked on. In that regard, it’s no different than when we explored the history of the Vietnam War, the Second World War, the Holocaust – any [Ken Burns] film. It’s been really important to me to take great care with the people who share their stories with us. I want to be fully present if we’re interviewing someone who has a difficult or tragic story to tell, and to keep an open mind and open heart. Just create space for them to share their truth and not judge them in that moment.
Q: What has it meant to collaborate with Ken Burns?
I’ve learned so much from him and gained so much incredible experience working on films about such a wide range of topics. What’s most exciting about collaborating is that you’re in a room with people who have many talents and ideas and feelings about what would make the best possible film, and you really hash it out with a goal to make the best film you know how to make. We argue, we debate, we listen, we try different things, and what’s really wonderful is to know that when we arrive at the right answer, we all can recognize that’s the best way to solve this particular [question]. There’s so many choices that we have to make and there’s really no ego involved. It’s really about serving the project.
It’s been a great privilege to work with Ken Burns for so many years. I started out as an associate producer on the Civil War series in 1989, so that is a long time. He’s also been incredibly supportive and generous to encourage me to continue working with him and to also go out and make films on my own.
